extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and creators interested in satire and media (e.g., those studying or producing satirical news)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract evaluative principles and standards illustrated by a Wikipedia profile of a single satirical news website (The Babylon Bee). Useful for assessing satire practices, moderation risk, and legal/ethical concerns about parody sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of satire: prompt self-reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: As Adam Ford described: satire's purpose is not just to evoke laughter but to 'examine ourselves.' 'Satire acts like an overhead projector, taking something that people usually ignore and projecting it up on the wall for everyone to see. It forces us to look at things we wouldn't normally look at and makes us ask if we're okay with them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use satire to highlight and provoke reflection about cultural, political, or religious behaviors; aim for insight as well as humor. Examples from the page: articles lampooning churchgoers or evangelical idiosyncrasies that encourage readers to reconsider practices or beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target selection and 'punching' balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The site's editorial stance described by editor Kyle Mann: 'this comedy makes fun of everybody, but it's a little harder on the left, and when it makes fun of the right it's not hateful.' Also described mission: 'mock[ing] people who hold cultural power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider who the satire targets (cultural power holders vs. marginalized groups) and the ethical tone (punch up vs. punch down). Aim to 'mock people who hold cultural power' rather than attack vulnerable populations; strive to avoid hateful content when targeting less-powerful groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and context to avoid being mistaken for factual news
rubrics_metrics.description: The page documents repeated instances where Babylon Bee pieces were mistaken for real news: researchers found people 'regularly mistook satirical reports... for genuine news'; press coverage notes headlines being rephrased or 'stripped of both context and comedy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure contextual signals (tone, framing, disclaimers, obvious absurdity) are present if the intent is clearly satirical. Be aware that headlines or stripped excerpts can be misread; wording and context are crucial to preserving satirical intent and reducing misinformation risk. Examples: Joel Osteen yacht piece and other viral items that were fact-checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checker treatment and the 'labeled satire' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Snopes' 'labeled satire' explanation: 'This rating indicates that a claim is derived from content described by its creator and/or the wider audience as satire. Not all content described by its creator or audience as 'satire' necessarily constitutes satire, and this rating does not make a distinction between 'real' satire and content that may not be effectively recognized or understood as satire despite being labeled as such.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that fact-checkers may treat content labeled as satire differently than straightforward false claims; however, labeling does not absolve creators of responsibility for clarity or potential deception. Expect fact-checkers to evaluate both origin/label and recognizability of satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid targeting marginalized groups or producing 'ironically' harmful material
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques cited: the site 'frequently makes jokes that target marginalized groups, with articles that are "often 'ironically' misogynistic" and "frequently antagonistic toward the LGBTQIA+ community".'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether irony actually shields content from harm or instead reinforces stereotypes. Be cautious with jokes about marginalized groups; consider how readers will interpret irony and whether the satire amplifies harmful tropes (example controversies cited on the page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of referential and layered irony (risk of reinforcing misinformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers noted the site's approach as 'riffs on riffs, building referential jokes atop the already referential right-wing commentary about the untrustworthiness of the news' and producing 'ironically ambiguous material' that can let audiences 'reinforce their own beliefs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layered, referential humor can be clever but increases the chance audiences will interpret content as confirmation of preexisting beliefs or misinformation. When using meta- or referential jokes, weigh comedic payoff against the risk of enabling confirmation bias or spreading false impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial focus and signature targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage notes: the site's 'signature hits focus on what the writers see as shallowness in the evangelical world' and it 'excels at poking fun at the small idiosyncrasies of believers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define and cultivate consistent targets or themes (e.g., institutional shallow practices) that shape the site's comedic voice. Signature focus helps set audience expectations but may also narrow perceived scope and invite repeated critique from those targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform moderation standards: incitement, hate speech, and hateful conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The article records removals/flags by Facebook and Twitter citing policies against 'incitement to violence', 'hate speech', or 'hateful conduct' (e.g., Facebook demonetized or removed posts; Twitter suspended account for alleged hateful conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical creators must account for platform policies; content that platforms interpret as incitement or hate speech—even if satirical—may be removed, demonetized, or lead to account actions. When pushing boundaries, expect moderation risk and consider appeals or public responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and First Amendment considerations for parody
rubrics_metrics.description: The Babylon Bee has participated in litigation and amicus briefs defending parody and parody-rights; courts and briefs argued that laws or enforcement that target parody can 'unconstitutionally stifle the free and unfettered exchange of ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that parody and satire enjoy strong First Amendment protections in many U.S. contexts, but legal outcomes depend on jurisdiction and specific statutes (e.g., 'hateful conduct' or deepfake/anti-disinformation laws). Be prepared for legal challenges and engage with counsel and amici when statutes or enforcement threaten satirical expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virality and audience metrics as indicators of success and of misinterpretation risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The page cites traffic figures (millions of page views per month) and notes that high sharing sometimes correlated with the site's pieces being mistaken as factual and subject to fact-checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High reach is a success metric but elevates responsibility: widely shared satire can be more likely to be misinterpreted and to trigger fact-checks or moderation. Monitor engagement and public response, and consider clearer labeling or contextual content for highly viral pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context preservation in excerpting or republication
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason's critique: headlines used in studies had been 'stripped of both context and comedy', and reworded headlines changed respondents' perceptions—showing context changes recognition of satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When quoting or sharing satire, preserve surrounding context (original headline phrasing, article body, site label) because excerpting or paraphrasing can remove comedic signals and convert satire into misleading content. Researchers and platforms should avoid decontextualized excerpts when assessing or presenting satirical material.
